questions.stem: A bad debt is best described as:
options: an estimate of the share of next year's credit sales that may not be paid
an amount owed by a customer that the business decides will never be collected
an amount the business owes a supplier that it has decided not to pay at all
a customer's account that is only a few days past its normal credit terms
questions.explanation: A bad debt is a specific accounts receivable balance judged uncollectable, for example because the customer is bankrupt. A slightly overdue account may still be collected, and an estimate of future non-payment is the idea behind the provision for doubtful debts.

questions.stem: Coral Coast Tiles has no provision for doubtful debts. A customer owing $800 is declared bankrupt and the debt is written off. Ignoring GST, which entry is recorded?
options: Dr Bad Debts 800; Cr Accounts Receivable 800
Dr Accounts Receivable 800; Cr Bad Debts 800
Dr Bad Debts 800; Cr Sales 800
Dr Accounts Payable 800; Cr Bad Debts 800
questions.explanation: Writing off the debt recognises an expense and removes the asset, so Bad Debts is debited and Accounts Receivable credited. Crediting Sales would wrongly reduce revenue that was genuinely earned when the sale was made.

questions.stem: What is the effect on the accounting equation of writing off a bad debt of $800 when there is no provision for doubtful debts?
options: Assets +$800; Liabilities nil; Owner's equity +$800
Assets −$800; Liabilities nil; Owner's equity −$800
Assets −$800; Liabilities −$800; Owner's equity nil
Assets nil; Liabilities nil; Owner's equity −$800
questions.explanation: Accounts receivable falls by $800, and the Bad Debts expense reduces profit and therefore owner's equity by $800. No liability is involved, because the business is not owed anything by a creditor.

questions.stem: In the Statement of Profit or Loss, bad debts recovered is reported as:
options: a reduction of the cost of goods sold for the year
a financing activity, because cash has been received
an increase in the provision for doubtful debts
other revenue, because it increases owner's equity
questions.explanation: Recovering an amount previously written off increases owner's equity, so it is reported as other revenue. The cash receipt appears in the Statement of Cash Flows, but the Statement of Profit or Loss shows the revenue.

questions.stem: A customer whose $600 debt was written off last year unexpectedly pays in full. Why is the debt usually reinstated in Accounts Receivable before the receipt is recorded?
options: so that last year's Statement of Profit or Loss can be reopened and its bad debts corrected
so that the cash received is reported as a financing inflow rather than an operating inflow
so that the business can charge interest on the full amount for the whole period overdue
so the customer's account shows the debt was eventually paid, which matters for future credit
questions.explanation: Reinstating the debt and then recording the receipt leaves a complete record in the customer's account, which helps when deciding whether to give that customer credit again. Last year's statements are not reopened; the recovery is revenue of the current period.

questions.stem: Coral Coast Tiles charges simple interest of 1.5% a month on overdue accounts. A customer's $2,000 account is two months overdue. No GST applies to interest. Which entry records the interest charged?
options: Dr Accounts Receivable 30; Cr Interest Revenue 30
Dr Bank 60; Cr Interest Revenue 60
Dr Accounts Receivable 60; Cr Interest Revenue 60
Dr Interest Expense 60; Cr Accounts Receivable 60
questions.explanation: 2,000 × 1.5% × 2 months = $60, added to the customer's debt and recognised as revenue earned. The bank is not debited because the interest has been charged but not yet received, and one month's interest would be only $30.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of charging interest on overdue accounts, and its immediate effect on the reports?
options: to encourage prompt payment; revenue and accounts receivable rise, but cash is unchanged until paid
to cover bank fees; expenses fall and the bank balance rises as soon as the interest is charged
to replace the provision for doubtful debts; the provision falls by the interest charged
to raise sales; net sales and cost of goods sold both rise by the amount of the interest
questions.explanation: Interest gives customers a reason to pay on time, and charging it increases interest revenue and accounts receivable. There is no cash inflow until the customer actually pays, so the bank balance is unchanged at the time of charging.

questions.stem: A provision for doubtful debts is created at the end of the period mainly to:
options: reduce the amount of GST the business must pay to the Australian Taxation Office
match the expected loss on credit sales with the period in which those sales were made
record the specific customers who have already been declared bankrupt during the year
set aside cash in a separate bank account to cover customers who do not pay later
questions.explanation: Under the accounting period concept and accrual accounting, the estimated cost of debts that will not be collected belongs to the period of the sales. The provision is a bookkeeping estimate, not a separate bank account, and known bad debts are written off instead.

questions.stem: In the Statement of Financial Position, the Provision for Doubtful Debts is reported as:
options: a non-current asset because it relates to debts collected in future years
an expense deducted from net sales to calculate the gross profit
a negative asset deducted from Accounts Receivable in current assets
a current liability owed to customers who may not pay their accounts
questions.explanation: The provision reduces accounts receivable to the amount expected to be collected, so it is a negative asset beside Accounts Receivable. It is not owed to anyone, so it is not a liability; the expense side of the entry is Doubtful Debts.

questions.stem: Why is the provision for doubtful debts kept in a separate account rather than credited directly to Accounts Receivable?
options: Accounts Receivable can only ever be credited when a customer pays the business in cash
the customers who will not pay are not yet known, so no individual account can be reduced
the law requires every business to keep a separate bank account for doubtful customers
it is a liability, so it must be kept apart from all of the business's asset accounts
questions.explanation: The provision is an estimate across all debtors; no specific customer has yet failed to pay, so individual balances cannot be written down. Keeping it separate preserves the full amount owed while still reporting the expected collectable amount.

questions.stem: At its first balance day, Coral Coast Tiles has accounts receivable of $48,000 and creates a provision for doubtful debts of 5% of accounts receivable. Which entry is recorded?
options: Dr Bad Debts 2,400; Cr Bank 2,400
Dr Doubtful Debts 2,400; Cr Provision for Doubtful Debts 2,400
Dr Provision for Doubtful Debts 2,400; Cr Doubtful Debts 2,400
Dr Doubtful Debts 2,400; Cr Accounts Receivable 2,400
questions.explanation: 5% × 48,000 = $2,400. The expense Doubtful Debts is debited and the negative asset account Provision for Doubtful Debts is credited. Crediting Accounts Receivable would wrongly treat unidentified customers as already written off.

questions.stem: The Provision for Doubtful Debts has a credit balance of $1,800. At balance day accounts receivable are $52,000 and the provision is to be 4% of accounts receivable. What is the balance day adjustment?
options: increase the provision by $280
increase the provision by $2,080
decrease the provision by $280
increase the provision by $3,880
questions.explanation: The required provision is 4% × 52,000 = $2,080. With $1,800 already in the account, only a further $280 is needed. Recording the full $2,080 would leave the provision at $3,880, overstating the expense.

questions.stem: After that adjustment, at what amount is Accounts Receivable reported (net) in the Statement of Financial Position?
questions.explanation: Net accounts receivable = 52,000 − 2,080 = $49,920, the amount expected to be collected. Deducting the old provision of $1,800 gives $50,200, which ignores the adjustment.

questions.stem: The Provision for Doubtful Debts has a credit balance of $3,000, but at balance day the required provision is only $2,500. What adjustment is needed, and what is its effect on net profit?
options: increase the provision by $2,500, which decreases net profit
decrease the provision by $500, which decreases net profit
no adjustment, because a provision is never reduced
decrease the provision by $500, which increases net profit
questions.explanation: The provision must be brought down to $2,500, a reduction of $500. Reducing an over-estimate lowers the period's doubtful debts cost, so net profit increases. A provision is adjusted up or down each balance day to the required amount.

questions.stem: Recording the year's doubtful debts expense of $2,080 affects which figures?
options: net cash from operating activities falls; net profit is unchanged until the debts are written off
current liabilities rise by $2,080 and owner's equity is unchanged
net profit and net accounts receivable fall; net cash from operating activities is unchanged
net profit and the bank balance both fall by $2,080 on balance day
questions.explanation: Doubtful debts is a non-cash expense: it reduces profit and the net value of accounts receivable, but no cash leaves the business. It is one reason net profit can be lower than net cash from operating activities.

questions.stem: Which is a reason a physical stocktake might show less inventory than the perpetual inventory records?
options: a supplier allowing longer credit terms for purchases
the owner contributing extra capital in cash
an increase in the provision for doubtful debts
theft, damage or recording errors during the period
questions.explanation: Discrepancies between the count and the records arise from theft, breakage, spoilage or errors in recording. Credit terms, capital contributions and the provision affect other accounts, not the quantity of goods on hand.

questions.stem: The inventory records of Mango Lane Homewares show $42,000, but the stocktake values inventory on hand at $41,200. Which entry adjusts the records?
options: Dr Cost of Goods Sold 41,200; Cr Inventory 41,200
Dr Drawings 800; Cr Inventory 800
Dr Inventory Loss 800; Cr Inventory 800
Dr Inventory 800; Cr Inventory Gain 800
questions.explanation: The records overstate inventory by $800, so Inventory is credited and the loss recognised as an expense. Recording a gain would be the entry if the count exceeded the records, and drawings applies only when the owner takes goods.

questions.stem: Mango Lane Homewares has 30 lamps that cost $50 each. They were damaged and can now be sold for $55 each, but only after repairs of $12 each. What inventory write-down is needed under lower of cost or net realisable value?
options: nil
questions.explanation: Net realisable value = 55 − 12 = $43, which is $7 below the cost of $50, so the write-down is 7 × 30 = $210. Ignoring the repair costs makes NRV $55, above cost, which would wrongly suggest no write-down is needed.

questions.stem: A line of cushions cost $20 each and can be sold for $26 each after selling costs of $1 each. At what value are they reported?
options: $25 each, their net realisable value, because it is the higher figure
$26 each, their expected selling price, because the market sets value
$19 each, cost less the selling costs, to be conservative
$20 each, their cost, because cost is below net realisable value
questions.explanation: Inventory is reported at the lower of cost ($20) and net realisable value (26 − 1 = $25). Cost is lower, so it is used; reporting the higher figure would record a profit before any sale is made.

questions.stem: What is the effect of recording an inventory write-down to net realisable value?
options: expenses rise, net profit falls and current assets fall, with no change in cash
cost of goods sold falls, net profit rises and the bank balance falls
current liabilities rise and owner's equity is unchanged
net cash from operating activities falls by the amount of the write-down
questions.explanation: The write-down is an expense that reduces profit and the inventory asset. No cash is paid, so cash flows are unaffected. Owner's equity falls along with profit.

questions.stem: Reversing entries are recorded:
options: only when an error has been found in the ledger
after the financial statements of the next year
on the first day of the new accounting period
on balance day, before the adjusted trial balance
questions.explanation: Reversing entries are made at the start of the new period to cancel certain balance day adjustments. They are not corrections of errors, and they are not recorded on balance day itself.

questions.stem: The main purpose of reversing entries is to:
options: correct errors in balance day adjustments that were found during the audit
transfer the net profit for the year to the owner's capital account
let the next payment or receipt be recorded normally, without splitting it between periods
remove all of last year's revenue and expenses from the ledger before new transactions
questions.explanation: By reversing an accrual, the full amount of the later payment or receipt can be recorded in the usual account, and the ledger automatically shows only the new period's share. Transferring profit to capital is done by closing entries.

questions.stem: At 30 June, Coral Coast Tiles recorded accrued wages of $3,000. Which reversing entry is recorded on 1 July?
options: Dr Accrued Wages 3,000; Cr Bank 3,000
Dr Wages 3,000; Cr Bank 3,000
Dr Accrued Wages 3,000; Cr Wages 3,000
Dr Wages 3,000; Cr Accrued Wages 3,000
questions.explanation: The reversing entry is the balance day adjustment back to front: Accrued Wages is debited to clear the liability and Wages is credited. The second option repeats the balance day adjustment, and the bank is not involved because nothing has yet been paid.

questions.stem: After that reversing entry, Coral Coast Tiles pays wages of $5,000 on 5 July, including the $3,000 earned in June. The payment is debited in full to Wages. What is the balance of the Wages account after the payment?
options: $8,000 debit
$2,000 debit
$5,000 debit
$3,000 credit
questions.explanation: The reversing entry left Wages with a $3,000 credit; the $5,000 debit brings it to a $2,000 debit, which is exactly July's share of the wages. Without the reversing entry the account would show $5,000, overstating July's expense.

questions.stem: At 30 June, accrued interest revenue of $400 was recorded on a term deposit. Which reversing entry is recorded on 1 July?
options: Dr Bank 400; Cr Accrued Interest Revenue 400
Dr Interest Revenue 400; Cr Bank 400
Dr Interest Revenue 400; Cr Accrued Interest Revenue 400
Dr Accrued Interest Revenue 400; Cr Interest Revenue 400
questions.explanation: The balance day adjustment debited the asset Accrued Interest Revenue, so the reversal credits it and debits Interest Revenue. When the interest is later received in full, the revenue account will then show only the new period's share.

questions.stem: Which balance day adjustment is NOT reversed at the start of the next period?
options: accrued interest on a loan
depreciation of equipment
accrued wages owing to staff
accrued rent revenue
questions.explanation: Depreciation has no later payment or receipt to record, and accumulated depreciation simply continues to build, so it is never reversed. Accrued expenses and accrued revenues are reversed so that the later cash flow can be recorded normally.

questions.stem: Which sequence is correct at the end of one period and the start of the next?
options: adjusted trial balance, reversing entries, balance day adjustments, closing entries
balance day adjustments, adjusted trial balance, closing entries, reversing entries
closing entries, balance day adjustments, reversing entries, adjusted trial balance
reversing entries, balance day adjustments, closing entries, adjusted trial balance
questions.explanation: Balance day adjustments update the accounts, the adjusted trial balance checks them and supports the statements, closing entries clear the revenue and expense accounts, and reversing entries are made on the first day of the new period.

questions.stem: Which accounts are closed at the end of the accounting period?
options: accounts receivable and accounts payable
revenue, expense and drawings accounts
asset, liability and capital accounts
accumulated depreciation and provision accounts
questions.explanation: Revenue and expense accounts are closed so the next period starts from zero, and drawings is closed to capital. Assets, liabilities, capital and negative asset accounts carry forward their balances into the new period.

questions.stem: After the closing entries, a business's revenues total $180,000 and expenses total $150,500. Opening capital was $70,000 and drawings were $22,000. What is the closing balance of Capital?
questions.explanation: Net profit = 180,000 − 150,500 = $29,500. Closing capital = 70,000 + 29,500 − 22,000 = $77,500. Forgetting to close drawings gives $99,500.

questions.stem: A new computer bought for $1,200 was debited to Office Expenses instead of Office Equipment. What type of error is this?
options: an error that the trial balance will reveal as a difference
a conceptual error, because an asset was recorded as an expense
a clerical error, because two digits of the amount were swapped
a consequential error, because it flowed from a wrong ledger balance
questions.explanation: Recording capital expenditure as an expense breaks an accounting principle, so it is a conceptual error. The amounts and both sides are still recorded, so the trial balance still agrees and will not reveal it.

questions.stem: Ignoring GST, which entry corrects the computer error, and what was the effect of the error if left uncorrected?
options: Dr Office Expenses 1,200; Cr Office Equipment 1,200; profit and assets were overstated
Dr Office Equipment 1,200; Cr Bank 1,200; cash was overstated and profit unchanged
Dr Office Equipment 2,400; Cr Office Expenses 2,400; profit was understated twice
Dr Office Equipment 1,200; Cr Office Expenses 1,200; profit and assets were understated
questions.explanation: The asset must be debited and the wrongly charged expense credited. Until corrected, expenses were overstated, so profit was understated, and the asset was missing, so assets were understated. The payment itself was recorded correctly, so Bank is not involved.

questions.stem: A payment of $540 was recorded as $450 in both the journal and the two ledger accounts. What kind of error is this, and will the trial balance reveal it?
options: a clerical error that makes the debit column $90 larger than the credit column
a consequential error that makes both columns of the trial balance $990 larger
a clerical transposition error that the trial balance will not reveal
a conceptual error that the trial balance will reveal immediately
questions.explanation: Swapping digits is a clerical error. Because the same wrong amount was debited and credited, both columns are understated by the same $90 and the trial balance still agrees.

questions.stem: A ledger balance is miscalculated, and the wrong balance is then carried into the trial balance and the Statement of Financial Position. The errors in the trial balance and statement are best described as:
options: conceptual errors, because an accounting principle was broken
errors of omission, because a transaction was never recorded
compensating errors, because two equal errors cancel each other
consequential errors, because they follow from the earlier error
questions.explanation: A consequential error is caused by an earlier error flowing through to later records. No principle was broken and nothing was omitted, so the conceptual and omission labels do not fit.

questions.stem: In the complete accounting process, what follows the recording of transactions in the general journal?
options: preparing the Statement of Financial Position
recording the reversing entries
collecting the source documents
posting the entries to the general ledger
questions.explanation: Source documents are collected first, entries are journalised, then posted to the ledger, which is balanced and checked with a trial balance before adjustments and reports. Reversing entries come at the start of the next period.

questions.stem: Under the qualitative characteristic of relevance, information is material if:
options: it is supported by a source document such as a tax invoice or receipt
it is prepared using the same methods as in the previous year
it is presented clearly enough for a user to understand without training
leaving it out or misstating it could influence the decisions of users
questions.explanation: Materiality, part of relevance, asks whether an item is big enough or important enough to change users' decisions. Support by source documents relates to reliability, and consistent methods relate to comparability.

questions.stem: A business records depreciation using the same method each year so the owner can compare its reports over time. Which qualitative characteristic does this support?
options: comparability
materiality
understandability
relevance
questions.explanation: Applying the same methods each period allows users to compare results over time and with other businesses, which is comparability. Understandability is about clear presentation to users with reasonable knowledge.

questions.stem: An accountant reports the cost of the shop's inventory from supplier invoices rather than the owner's guess of its value. Which qualitative characteristic is most directly applied?
options: reliability, because the figure is free from bias and can be verified
understandability, because invoices are easy for any user to read
comparability, because invoices are kept in date order each period
materiality, because inventory is the largest current asset
questions.explanation: Reliable information is free from bias and error and can be checked against evidence such as source documents. An owner's estimate could be biased, so it is less reliable.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of the Statement of Financial Position as a measure of a business's worth?
options: most assets are shown at historical cost, and items like reputation and staff skill are not shown
it reports only the cash received and paid during the period, not the assets and liabilities
it cannot show liabilities that are owed for longer than twelve months after balance day
it reports only revenue and expenses, so it says nothing about the owner's equity
questions.explanation: Assets are generally recorded at historical cost less depreciation rather than current market value, and internally developed assets such as reputation are not recorded, so the statement can understate what the business is worth. It does show non-current liabilities and owner's equity.

questions.stem: Why is net profit in the Statement of Profit or Loss described as an estimate rather than an exact figure?
options: it depends on estimates such as depreciation, doubtful debts and inventory values
it is rounded to the nearest thousand dollars under the materiality principle
it includes the GST collected on sales, which may later be refunded
it is based only on cash received, so credit sales are left out
questions.explanation: Expenses like depreciation, doubtful debts and inventory write-downs rely on judgements about useful life, residual value, collections and selling prices, so profit is partly an estimate. It is prepared on an accrual basis, so credit sales are included and GST is excluded from revenue.
